name: Familiarity heuristic
statement: When two objects are both recognised, people infer that the more familiar one ranks higher on whatever is being judged.
meaning: Three different claims travel under this name and they do not share a literature. The first is the one bias lists print: the familiar is favoured over the novel, and familiar things feel safer, better and more common. No paper was found that defines or tests that claim under that name. The second is a rule for binary choice, proposed by Hidehito Honda and colleagues and modelled formally: given two cities, pick the more familiar as the larger. That rule generalises Goldstein and Gigerenzer's recognition heuristic, which can only fire when one of the two objects is unrecognised, and it has been tested against knowledge-based models. The third is the cue-familiarity heuristic in metamemory, where the familiarity of a question, rather than anything retrieved about its answer, drives the feeling of knowing the answer. The second and third claims each have evidence. Neither of them is the first one.

origin.note: Their paper is "The role of familiarity in binary choice inferences" and it calls the rule familiarity-based inference. Honda's later papers call the same rule the familiarity heuristic. The cue-familiarity heuristic of metamemory is older and separate: Koriat and Levy-Sadot's abstract traces it to Reder's 1987 paper on strategy selection in question answering.

evidence: Honda and colleagues ran two experiments on city populations. In the first, 33 undergraduates, all women, at Japan Women's University rated how familiar city names were and then chose which of two cities was larger. The mean proportion of choices agreeing with familiarity-based inference was 0.791, SD = 0.105. In the second, 81 undergraduates from the same university split into three clusters by how sensitive they were to small differences in familiarity, with mean agreement of 0.865, SD = 0.046, then 0.623, SD = 0.092, then 0.764, SD = 0.058. Their abstract reports that where participants had cue knowledge about population, they used it instead of familiarity. Honda, Matsuka and Ueda then set heuristic models against knowledge-based models on the same kind of task. Their abstract reports that a familiarity heuristic model explained inferences on tasks participants found subjectively difficult, and a knowledge-based model explained the ones they found easy. The metamemory strand is separate work. Metcalfe, Schwartz and Joaquim repeated cue words a varying number of times while holding the memorability of the targets apart from that count. With 30 Dartmouth students, cued recall ran .39, .33, .17 and .19 across the four conditions and recognition ran .72, .56, .59 and .48, while feeling-of-knowing ratings tracked neither, following instead the number of times the cue had been shown, F(3, 87) = 12.64.

replication.headline: An independent laboratory in Ohio reproduced the binary-choice rule with different cities and a formal model, and 62% of choices between two invented city names went to the more familiar name.
replication.detail: Xu, Gonzalez-Vallejo, Weinhardt, Chimeli and Karadogan tested the familiarity difference cue on Ohio cities rather than Japanese ones. Their stimuli were 24 large Ohio cities, 24 small ones and 24 invented names. In their first study, 113 Ohio University undergraduates rated familiarity and then made 72 paired choices about city size. Of the 113, 111 showed a significant positive correlation between city size and their own familiarity ratings, which is 98.23%. The invented names are the clean test, because nothing can be known about a city that does not exist. Of 1,356 pairs of two invented names, 944 were rated equally familiar. Of the remaining 412, participants chose the more familiar name 255 times, or 62%. In their second study, 50 undergraduates gave data that the r-s multinomial model fitted well, G-squared(3) = 1.23, p = .75. Their conclusion is that participants ignored further knowledge in a substantial number of cases when the familiarity difference cue was available. Response times were shorter for heuristic judgments than for judgments made on knowledge. What has been reproduced is the narrow rule about comparative judgment. The bias-list claim that familiar options feel safer was not tested by any of this work.

study.cite: Xu, P., González-Vallejo, C., Weinhardt, J., Chimeli, J., & Karadogan, F. (2018). Use of the familiarity difference cue in inferential judgments. Memory & Cognition, 46(2), 298-314.

limits: The rule is bounded by knowledge on one side and by its own materials on the other. Honda and colleagues report that cue knowledge about population displaced familiarity where participants had it, and Honda, Matsuka and Ueda report that the knowledge-based model won on tasks people found easy. Every study named here judges the size of cities. Familiarity is measured by asking the same person who then makes the choice, so cue and criterion come from one source. The samples are 33 and 81 women at one Japanese university and 113 and 50 undergraduates at Ohio University. No meta-analysis and no multi-laboratory replication of the familiarity heuristic was located. On the bias-list claim, that familiar things are judged safer or better, no paper was found that states and tests it under that name. That search covered Crossref by bibliographic query for the phrase, OpenAlex by title, PubMed, and general web search. The Wikipedia article of that name cites nine references, and none of them carries the phrase in its title or studies a thing so called. Honda's 2020 analysis of how forgetting affects the heuristic is a computer simulation in ACT-R, published as an invited article in a university philosophy journal, and it produces no human data.
misreadings: The commonest error is to run the arrow backwards. Monin reports five studies in which positive valence raises how familiar something feels with no prior exposure at all, so that attractive faces feel familiar, and he calls this the warm glow heuristic. Wikipedia's familiarity heuristic article cites that paper. Liking causing felt familiarity is not familiarity causing liking, and only the second is what the name promises. A second error is treating the rule as the recognition heuristic under another label. Goldstein and Gigerenzer's heuristic fires on missing knowledge, when one object is recognised and the other is not, and the familiarity rule was proposed for the pairs the recognition heuristic cannot reach. A third is borrowing the availability literature. Judging a class more frequent because famous instances come to mind is Tversky and Kahneman's own study 8, which this atlas records under the availability heuristic, and it is not evidence for a separate rule. A fourth is treating the metamemory strand as the same thing. Its central prediction has taken a hit that the binary-choice strand has not: Oliver, Li, Harley and Humphreys ran three experiments and found that tip-of-the-tongue states repeated whether or not the second prompt was the same cue as the first, which their abstract calls inconsistent with the cue familiarity hypothesis.
